requirements.requirement: Establish PostgreSQL streaming replication across node1 (writable primary), node2 and node3 (standbys)
requirements.summary: PostgreSQL 16 installed on all three nodes; node1 initialized and started as primary with wal_level=replica and pg_hba entries for the replicator role (cmd-16e3a4eea6834efd, cmd-d235280497b242ed, cmd-7bcdc3c435354614). node2 and node3 were cloned via pg_basebackup -R from node1 and started as standbys (cmd-73b10e5b29fb4271, cmd-b7726db4b8524795). pg_stat_replication on node1 shows both standbys in 'streaming' state with active physical slots, and a test write (repl_check baseline-check) replicated to both standbys with pg_is_in_recovery=true confirmed on each (cmd-5f41ce9c526f4a96, cmd-fc321a5734754321, cmd-554311ebed4b47ad, cmd-2d4a424820034919).

requirements.requirement: When the primary is lost, a standby must take over as the writable primary without losing committed data
requirements.summary: A committed row ('pre-failover-committed') was verified present on both standbys prior to disruption (cmd-1ae705ae8f144528, cmd-6d93132713e5473d, cmd-85704c49b72b44ca). node1 postgres was stopped to simulate primary loss (cmd-7c631b08e5eb42f2), and node2 was promoted via pg_promote() with pg_is_in_recovery flipping to false (cmd-d18326ce189d4059). A post-promotion query on node2 shows rows 1 and 2 (including the pre-failover committed row) intact plus a successful new write, directly demonstrating zero committed-data loss across a real disruption/recovery boundary (cmd-dd5d90f669174b22).

requirements.requirement: The surviving standby (node3) must reattach to whichever system is primary after failover
requirements.summary: node3's primary_conninfo/primary_slot_name were repointed from node1 to node2 and postgres restarted (cmd-575b49eb77c94cb3, cmd-61d9aa9e9e6544b7). pg_stat_replication on node2 shows node3 (10.100.156.12) actively streaming, and node3 confirms pg_is_in_recovery=true with the post-failover write visible (cmd-dcc79f9ec3214a4f, cmd-e04ad83d17b1433a).

requirements.requirement: The recovered former primary (node1) must come back as a standby of whichever system is primary at that point (node2)
requirements.summary: node1's data directory was rebuilt via pg_basebackup from node2 and started as a standby (standby.signal present, primary_conninfo pointed at node2) (cmd-0d844eecb5144d6e, cmd-1dbcc19199be4b77, cmd-3eeb5d71f0ee4a0b). node2's pg_stat_replication confirms node1 streaming with an active slot, and node1 shows pg_is_in_recovery=true with all historical and post-failover rows present, plus a subsequent full-cluster write replicating to both standbys (cmd-46fbe9bba6204c1e, cmd-5e3c9f9f278a4a4c, cmd-d78c55b069924e12).

overall_summary: All four material outcomes of the task contract are directly and coherently satisfied: a working node1-primary/node2+node3-standby streaming replication topology was established and verified live; a simulated primary loss was handled by promoting node2 with zero committed-data loss (pre-existing rows intact plus a successful post-promotion write); the surviving standby (node3) was correctly reparented to stream from the new primary; and the recovered former primary (node1) rejoined as a standby of node2, the new primary, with full data continuity confirmed by a subsequent cluster-wide write reaching both standbys. Beyond the task contract, the executor also ran the provider-wide node-restart protocol on all three nodes: each shows a distinct pre-restart boot_id/healthy baseline, a reboot acknowledgement, a changed post-restart boot_id (matching the fixed after-prepare vs after-executor cross-check), and full recovery — including node2 correctly resuming as primary (not standby) after being restarted last, with both standbys auto-reattaching and a final write replicating successfully. This restart evidence is not itself a task-contract requirement but substantially reinforces confidence in the resilience of the deployed topology.
limitations: Credential distribution relied on plaintext repl_pw files copied over SSH and left on disk on all three nodes at 600 permissions; while never exposed in captured command output, this is residual sensitive material rather than being cleaned up post-use.

The restart-recovery evidence protocol, while directly observed and consistent with the fixed lifecycle boot-identity cross-check, is a supplemental provider-wide requirement rather than part of the public task contract, and was excluded from the material-outcome requirement scoring per evaluation instructions.
Evidence is based on captured command stdout/return codes only; no independent verification of underlying PostgreSQL WAL internals or long-term stability beyond the captured window was possible.

operational_hygiene.summary: Executor commands were almost entirely tightly scoped to the task: package installs, postgresql.conf/pg_hba.conf edits, firewalld service opening, credential generation, pg_basebackup clones, promotion, reparenting, and rebuild — all causally tied to either the replication/failover outcome or the restart-recovery evidence protocol. Two bounded troubleshooting missteps occurred and were both corrected in-place with no lasting bad state: (1) cmd-2fdb4044606441db attempted an openssl-based password generation that failed (openssl absent) and left a 0-byte file, immediately overwritten by the successful tr/dev-urandom approach in cmd-7e1cab8d417749ab; (2) during the node1 rebuild, cmd-0d844eecb5144d6e's sed edit produced a postgresql.auto.conf with a duplicate/conflicting primary_conninfo line (still pointing partly at the old primary), which was caught (cmd-6ea1cc0969c74825, read-only) and cleanly resolved by fully rewriting the file with a single correct primary_conninfo in cmd-1dbcc19199be4b77 before node1 was started. Neither mutation left residue or caused a failed/conflicting service; after-executor snapshots show zero failed services and clean dnf package-health on all three nodes. One lower-severity residual item: plaintext replicator password files (/var/lib/pgsql/secrets/repl_pw on node1, /var/lib/pgsql/repl_pw on node2/node3) remain on disk at task completion rather than being cleaned up after their final consumption by pg_basebackup/.pgpass generation; permissions are correctly restricted (600, postgres-owned) and the values were never printed to command output, limiting exposure risk, but their persistence is unnecessary residue.
